title: Black Sea Strikes Are Making It Harder to Get Wheat
summary:
Imagine a sea where ships are afraid to sail. That's the Black Sea right now, between Ukraine and Russia.

Since July, there have been more than 210 attacks on commercial ships — boats that carry goods, not soldiers. A British risk firm called Ambrey says Ukraine was behind 125 of those strikes and Russia 88. Both countries are trying to stop the other from selling grain.

Russia and Ukraine together grow about a quarter of the world's wheat. That's the grain used to make bread, pasta, and cereal. Because of the attacks, their combined wheat exports are down about 60 percent from last year. Fewer exports mean higher prices around the world.

Mykola Lupar, a 29-year-old Ukrainian navy commander, says his crew only has minutes on the water before they must rush back to shore. "It's very dangerous," he said.

Russia says it only targets military ships. Ukraine says Russia is hitting civilian ships, including one called the Golden Leo, where ten people were killed in July. Turkey has tried to arrange a truce, but so far it hasn't worked.
why_it_matters: Grain from the Black Sea becomes the bread, pasta and cereal in kitchens everywhere, so trouble on that sea can make breakfast cost more and make food harder to find for kids in other countries.

background_read: The Black Sea (a sea between Europe and Asia, bordered by countries like Ukraine, Russia and Turkey) is one of the world's main routes for shipping food.
Ukraine and Russia are sometimes called the 'breadbasket' of Europe because their huge farms grow so much wheat, and a lot of that grain is sold to countries in Africa and the Middle East.
When ships cannot sail safely, countries far away can run short of food and pay more for bread — this is what happened when war made shipping in the Black Sea unsafe.
Article_Structure: WHO: Russia and Ukraine, who are attacking each other's ships in the Black Sea, plus Turkey trying to make peace.
WHAT: More than 210 attacks on commercial ships since July have cut the two countries' combined wheat exports by about 60 percent.
WHERE: The Black Sea, the sea between Ukraine and Russia, where grain ships normally sail.
WHY: Each side wants to stop the other from selling grain, so sailors are in danger and food prices rise around the world.
